papers.title: Retrieval practice is associated with attenuated stress-related inference impairment and stronger reactivation of bridge-related category information
papers.abstract: A hallmark of human memory is its ability to form novel inferences by linking discrete but related events. We examined whether acute stress impairs memory inference and if retrieval practice can buffer this effect. Participants were trained on image pairs, AB and BC, to establish interconnected triads (ABC) with a shared bridge element B. Twenty-four hours later, we induced acute stress in half of the participants and then tested their capacity to infer the indirect AC associations. Behavioral results indicated that acute stress reduced inference accuracy and slowed responses, and retrieval practice was associated with attenuation of stress-induced impairment in A-C inference accuracy and speed. Using multivariate decoding analysis of human electroencephalogram (EEG) recordings, we found neural evidence of rapid reactivation of bridge-related category information during inference, a neural signature predictive of subsequent successful inference. Importantly, stress was associated with reduced bridge-related category reactivation, whereas retrieval practice was associated with stronger reactivation under stress. Collectively, our findings link rapid reactivation of bridge-related category information to successful memory-based inference. Although susceptible to stress, this reactivation was stronger following retrieval practice, suggesting that robust memory traces may contribute to more resilient inference under stress.

papers.title: Originality in creative ideation evolves along nonlinear axes in the human brain
papers.abstract: The ability to think creatively is fundamental to human cognition, shaping how we interact with the world and navigate complex problems. Creativity depends on the activity of multiple large-scale brain networks, but the neural representations that underlie creative thought and distinguish it from other cognitive states remains unclear. Here, we use multiscale intracranial electrophysiology--from single-unit recordings to local field potentials across distributed brain networks--to discover how the human brain generates creative ideas. Our results demonstrate that cortical networks in the human brain display activity patterns that differentiate creative thinking from non-creative cognitive processes such as arithmetic calculations. We found that the underlying geometry of neural activity in the default mode network is shaped by instantaneous cognitive state. Further, in the dorsal attention network, we uncovered nonlinear, high-dimensional representations of moment-by-moment fluctuations in creative performance. These representations define a neural creativity axis that is shared between network-level and single-neuron computations. Our findings reveal widespread neural representations of cognitive state and suggest distinct roles of specific cortical networks in controlling creativity, with the default mode network enabling creative states, while higher-dimensional dorsal attention network activity, associated with attentional selection or other context-dependent constraints, reflects the production of more original responses.

papers.title: Expression-System Biases Compromise the Functional Assessment of KCNH2 Variants and Clinical Risk Assessment
papers.abstract: Background: Functional characterization of KCNH2 variants is essential for assessing pathogenicity in long QT syndrome type 2. Because hERG channels assemble as tetramers, the relative expression of wild-type (WT) and variant subunits critically influences channel function and pathogenicity assessment. However, commonly used experimental systems may not reproduce the balanced allelic expression observed in heterozygous patients. Methods: Allele-specific KCNH2 expression was analyzed in two independent RNA-sequencing datasets from human left ventricular tissue. Using the dominant-negative T74R hERG variant as a model, we calibrated the relationship between WT-to-variant expression ratios and hERG current amplitude. Using automated patch-clamp electrophysiology, we compared 3 dual-expression strategies: internal ribosome entry site (IRES), P2A-linked tandem constructs, and dual cytomegalovirus promoter (dCMV) constructs. Co-electroporation of WT and variant plasmids in different ratios was the reference. Results: Allele-specific expression analysis supported balanced KCNH2 expression in human left ventricular tissue. At a 1:1 WT-to-T74R expression ratio, hERG current amplitude was reduced to 31.0% of WT, consistent with a dominant-negative mechanism in which incorporation of 2 or more T74R subunits renders the channel nonfunctional. All 3 dual-expression strategies produced substantial expression imbalances, with the first cassette consistently favored. IRES constructs showed the greatest asymmetry. P2A constructs partially improved expression balance but introduced an additional N-terminal proline in the second cassette altering T74R-associated trafficking and channel biophysics. The dCMV system also failed to achieve balanced expression, including after stable integration. Co-electroporation of separate WT and variant plasmids provided the most reliable means of controlling their relative expression. Conclusions: Commonly used dual-expression constructs do not reliably reproduce balanced WT and variant hERG expression, potentially distorting assessments of dominant-negative effects and variant pathogenicity. Co-electroporation of separate plasmids provides a robust approach for high-throughput functional phenotyping under heterozygous conditions, with implications for the interpretation of KCNH2 variants and potentially other genes encoding multimeric ion channels.

papers.title: Next generation Human Neocortical Neurosolver model with biophysically realistic somatic, dendritic and synaptic dynamics
papers.abstract: The Human Neocortical Neurosolver (HNN) is an open-source biophysical modeling tool for multiscale interpretation of human electroencephalography (EEG) and magnetoencephalography (MEG) signals. HNN's foundation is a pre-tuned canonical neocortical circuit model consisting of excitatory pyramidal neurons and inhibitory interneurons in supra- (L2/3) and infragranular (L5) layers. This model was originally developed based on studies in rodent and non-human primate cortices when dynamics of human neurons were poorly characterized. Yet recent advances in recordings from human tissue now provide unprecedented detail to update the model. Here, we present a significantly updated model for use in the HNN software, with electrophysiological properties and synaptic connections tuned to human tissue. Beyond reproducing biologically realistic somatic dynamics, the pyramidal cells simulate dendritic calcium (Ca2+) spikes in the L5 extratelencephalic-projecting (ET) neurons, and shorter dendritic spikes in the L2/3 pyramidal neurons. We demonstrate how the updated circuitry and new features in the HNN software can be used to disentangle somatic, synaptic, and dendritic contributions to human E-/MEG signatures. The model is distributed with workflows to simulate event-related responses and oscillations, and tutorials demonstrating how membrane potentials, Ca2+ dynamics, and synaptic currents can be recorded and visualized. These enhancements allow extensive model validations based on in vitro and in vivo electrophysiology, voltage and Ca2+ imaging, and provide users with novel insights on the mechanisms underlying E-/MEG signals.

papers.title: A novel function of neuroligin 3: Beyond sociality, Regulating lifespan in Drosophila
papers.abstract: Neuroligins are conserved postsynaptic adhesion proteins involved in synaptic function and behaviour. In Drosophila melanogaster, Neuroligin 3 (Nlg3) regulates social behaviour, sleep and synaptic architecture. We now report, through analysis of publicly available transcriptomics data, confirmed with RT-qPCR data, that loss-of-function of the nlg3 gene downregulates the expression of longevity-associated genes foxo, hsp70s, and hsp68. Graded genetic manipulation of the Drosophila melanogaster neuroligin 3 (nlg3) gene indeed modulates both social spacing and lifespan. Specifically, reduced nlg3 expression (via heterozygous deletion, or transposable-element insertion) extends lifespan in both sexes, while overexpression or complete deletion shortens it. In contrast, overexpression or complete loss of nlg3 leads the flies to be further apart (increased social distance, or social space), as does RNAi knockdown, while heterozygous reduction of nlg3 expression either lowers or does not alter the flies social space. This work identifies a previously unrecognized link between a conserved synaptic gene, social behaviour, and organismal longevity.

papers.title: Sleep promotes neuronal autophagy for intracellular clearance
papers.abstract: Sleep is essential for brain health, yet how it maintains neuronal homeostasis at the cellular level remains poorly understood. Here, we show that extended wakefulness selectively suppressed neuronal autophagic flux in the cortex of mice, whereas sleep rapidly restored it, accompanied by a shift in autophagic cargo from mitochondrial components to synaptic proteins. Sleep upregulated ATG7 expression in the cortex, involving both lysosomal degradation and a putative noncanonical secretory route. Moreover, low neuronal activity is associated with efficient flux, as Gq-mediated neuronal activation impaired autophagy and promoted intracellular amyloid-beta; accumulation. Notably, closed-loop optogenetic stimulation of lysosomal acidification, exclusively during sleep, reduced amyloid pathology in 5xFAD mice, whereas wake-targeted stimulation worsened pathology. Together, these findings demonstrate that sleep serves as a physiological gatekeeper for cortical neuronal autophagy, and highlight the importance of brain-state timing for enhancing intracellular proteostasis in neurodegenerative disease.

papers.title: Variation in infant subcortical brain development from 6 to 12 months in Down syndrome
papers.abstract: Introduction: Down syndrome (DS), arising from Trisomy 21, is the most common genetic condition associated with intellectual disability. While smaller total brain volumes have been consistently observed in DS, no longitudinal neuroimaging studies have examined volumetric brain development in DS during infancy, a period of rapid neural growth when interventions may have the greatest impact. Method: High-resolution T1- and T2-weighted images were acquired during natural sleep in a multisite longitudinal cohort of 44 infants with DS and 39 control infants without DS at ages 6 and 12 months. Neuroimaging data were harmonized to reduce batch effects, and a novel deep-learning, repeated-measures segmentation approach was applied to optimize neuroanatomical segmentations. Total intracranial volume (ICV) and bilateral absolute subcortical volumes (amygdala, caudate, hippocampus, pallidum, putamen, thalamus) were first directly compared in infants with and without DS at 6 and 12 months. Hierarchical linear modeling (HLM) evaluated longitudinal group differences for each structure, accounting for sex, gestational age, and laterality. Subcortical group differences estimated by HLM were also compared to group differences in total ICV. Results: ICV in infants with DS was lower than controls at 6 months (12.6%; p<.001) and 12 months (16.3%; p<.001). Subcortical structures displayed a range of lower volumes (6.9%-13.1%; p's<.003) in infants with DS, although the caudate and putamen were exceptions. Caudate volumes were on average lower in DS but not significantly different from controls, while putamen volumes were on average higher in DS but not significantly different from controls, except for the right putamen, which was significantly larger (5.3%; p=.018) at 6 months. In HLM, ICV and all subcortical structures showed slower growth in DS from 6 to 12 months, except for the amygdala and putamen, which displayed similar growth rates to controls. DS-associated reductions in subcortical volumes were similar in magnitude to ICV, although 12-month caudate and 6- and 12-month putamen volumes were enlarged relative to ICV. Conclusion: Infants with DS exhibited substantially reduced ICV and widespread reductions in subcortical volumes and growth from 6-12 months. Across a range of volumetric differences, findings were most distinct in the basal ganglia, for which volume reductions were attenuated in the caudate, while the putamen was uniquely enlarged with comparable growth to controls. These observations support early regional specificity in the neural impact of Trisomy 21 and underscore the utility of infant neuroimaging to inform biologically based interventions and clinical trial readiness in DS.

papers.title: Cerebrospinal Fluid Inflammation in Prodromal Parkinson's Disease
papers.abstract: We hypothesized that prodromal Parkinson's disease (PD), characterized by rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder (RBD) and/or hyposmia, begins with inflammation in the central nervous system that evolves into neurodegeneration. We combined clinical phenotyping and proteomics with single-cell RNA sequencing of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and blood from individuals with RBD, PD, and healthy controls, with multiple sclerosis as a comparator. CSF immune cell numbers were increased in RBD, particularly in those with lower prodromal PD probability scores, a composite score associated with time to phenoconversion. In these participants, CSF macrophages showed enhanced TNF, IL-6/JAK/STAT3, and interferon-{gamma} signaling and predicted crosstalk with CD4+ T cells involving TNF, antigen presentation, and costimulatory pathways. CSF Macrophages resembled mouse dural macrophages and shared TNF signaling with gut immune cells from -synuclein mouse models. These findings uncover a stage-specific TNF-associated inflammation involving crosstalk between CSF Macrophages and CD4+ T cells in prodromal PD.

papers.title: Design and Test Novel EEG Electrode Attachments for Type 4 Afro-textured Hairstyles
papers.abstract: Black participants remain underrepresented in electroencephalography (EEG) research, partly because current EEG devices work poorly with dense, coily Type 4 Afro-textured hair. Research-grade EEG typically wires electrodes on a cap, and therefore the electrodes often fail to reach the scalp through dense, Afro-textured hair. Protocols that ask Black participants to unbraid or restyle protective hairstyles add burdens that discourage enrollment in research studies. To address this, we designed and tested 3D-printed attachments that fit onto an EEG electrode and anchored it directly in the hair, using the hairstyle itself as the mounting structure. We fabricated three design configurations for natural Afro-textured hair, cornrows/braids, and twists/microlocs. Seventeen healthy adults with Type 4a-4c hair used electrode attachments that matched their hairstyle. During a single visit, EEG was recorded with 16 conventional cap electrodes defined by the international 10-20 system and with 16 electrodes using novel electrode attachments anchored directly to their hair. Participants completed resting and walking trials with each system. Electrode-to-scalp distance and gel volume were measured during setup. Electrode disconnection, impedance, signal quality (i.e. peak alpha power and aperiodic (1/f) component), and comfort level were measured throughout the data collection. Compared with the conventional cap, the novel attachments reduced electrode-to-scalp distance, gel use, and impedance. Twenty percent of the conventional cap electrodes failed to connect to the scalp compared with 0.1% of novel electrodes. Impedance rose across trials for the conventional cap, whereas the novel attachments showed a smaller increase and maintained lower impedance throughout. Signal quality was significantly better using the novel attachments, while comfort level did not differ between systems. In conclusion, hair-anchored electrode attachment may present a feasible alternative to conventional cap-based EEG for people with Type 4 hair, yielding more usable channels and better signal quality, and supporting more inclusive EEG acquisition.

papers.title: Predictive stability code: Trial-by-trial conflict expectations tune task representations via proactive and reactive spatio-temporo-spectral dynamics
papers.abstract: Cognitive stability, or task focus, enables goal-directed behavior through representational dynamics: by prioritizing task-relevant representations over competing task-irrelevant ones. Beyond corrective reactive mechanisms operating after conflict arises, stability can also be engaged predictively through the statistical learning of conflict regularities, either proactively, based on global conflict expectations, or through a predictive reactive mode, guided by item-specific conflict expectations. Yet, the representational mechanisms enabling such predictive adjustments remain underspecified. We addressed this by re-analyzing EEG data from a spatial Stroop task concurrently manipulating list-wide (LWPC) and item-specific (ISPC) proportion congruency. Moving beyond existing analytical approaches, we developed a framework that combines trial-by-trial Bayesian conflict-expectancy modeling with a novel spatio-temporo-spectral searchlight Representational Similarity Analysis, and leveraged directional representational modeling complemented by ridge-regression decoding. We first identified the necessary computational substrate for predictive stability reconfigurations: the spatio-temporo-spectral patterns encoding task (Target, Distractor) and conflict-expectancy (LWPC, ISPC) representations, with the latter already encoded in the pre-stimulus windows. Crucially, conflict expectations modulated Target and Distractor encoding strength with distinct spatio-temporal and spectral dynamics, revealing a functional dissociation. LWPC-induced proactive stability follows a "Target-first" policy, primarily strengthening the Target representation early after stimulus onset via Alpha and lower-Beta patterns, and weakening Distractor encoding only later; conversely, ISPC-induced predictive reactive stability follows a "Distractor-first" policy, rapidly weakening Distractor encoding via response-locked posterior Beta patterns, and strengthening the Target representation only downstream. Our study refines theoretical cognitive control models, incorporating a mechanistic explanation for predictive stability, while also establishing a multidimensional methodological template for investigating the underlying substrates of adaptive behavior and beyond.

papers.title: Mice, marmosets and humans use ambiguous local motion to stabilize gaze
papers.abstract: Animals need to infer properties of the environment that are only ambiguously encoded by neurons in the sensory periphery. Can these ambiguous signals drive behavior directly, or must the ambiguity first be resolved? We traced motion signals from the retina through the nucleus of the optic tract (NOT) to reflexive eye movements, combining retinal and in vivo electrophysiology, computational modelling, and eye tracking in mice, marmosets and humans. Using stimuli that dissociate local edge motion from global, object motion, we found that responses of NOT neurons were strongly biased towards local motion. This bias propagated to behavior: eye movements followed local motion; in mice, to the point that changing the edge orientation of vertically moving objects produced horizontal eye movements. Marmosets and humans exhibited similar biases, amplified in humans when central vision was masked. Thus, the brain can transform ambiguous sensory signals directly into behavior, without first resolving the ambiguity.

papers.title: Closed-loop neurofeedback reshapes preparatory brain states to bias subsequent pain processing
papers.abstract: Pain perception is shaped not only by nociceptive input but also by neural activity preceding stimulation. Whether these preparatory states can be modified through neurofeedback, and whether such effects depend on feedback authenticity, remains unclear. We used a double-blind, sham-controlled 2 x 2 mixed factorial design, crossing active regulation versus passive observation with real versus sham EEG feedback. Across feedback groups, active training was associated with changes in preparatory EEG activity and reductions in pain intensity and unpleasantness. Compared with sham feedback, authentic EEG-contingent feedback produced greater enhancement of power in the targeted somatosensory cortex, also evident in source estimates of the right postcentral gyrus, and selectively reduced transitions from microstate E to D. Authentic feedback was also associated with greater attenuation of laser-evoked N2 and P2 responses and a larger reduction in pain intensity, but not unpleasantness. Exploratory structural equation modeling identified indirect associations linking feedback authenticity, preparatory and microstate changes, P2 attenuation, and pain-rating changes. Together, these findings provide experimental evidence that preparatory neural activity can be modulated through authentic neurofeedback and that this modulation is accompanied by changes in subsequent nociceptive processing, supporting a state-based account of pain.

papers.title: Reusing pipettes in Patch-seq: a foundation for automated multimodal profiling
papers.abstract: Patch-seq is a technique for single-cell multimodal characterization. It combines whole-cell electrophysiology, single-cell transcriptomics, and morphological reconstruction in single neurons. Patch-seq morphologies are a critical bridge among cell types, genes, physiology, and large-scale connectivity platforms such as EM connectomes and single-cell-resolution projectomes. However, patch-seq experimental complexity and operator dependence limit throughput. Automation could enable scalable Patch-seq but requires procedural adaptations, including detergent-based pipette cleaning, robotic nucleus extraction and collection. The impact of these automations on Patch-seq quality has not been systematically evaluated. Here, we show that each of these modifications preserves or improves key Patch-seq outcomes. Automated nucleus extraction performs comparably to, or better than, expert manual operation, preserving key RNA and morphological metrics. Detergent-cleaned, reused pipettes supported a viable sealing success rate across multiple cleaning cycles and preserved electrophysiological quality and transcriptomic yield without introducing excess contamination. Sonication effectively allows collection of nuclear material without damaging RNA and supports subsequent pipette cleaning and reuse. Enhanced automated sealing and break-in procedures increased throughput regardless of brain region, cell type or species. Together, these results validate the core procedural adaptations required for automated Patch-seq and establish a foundation for high-throughput, standardized multimodal single-cell characterization.

papers.title: The temporal dynamics of animacy-related neural representations are robust to controversial training
papers.abstract: Animal bias refers to the human tendency to prioritise the neural processing of animate over inanimate stimuli, a phenomenon observed across multiple cognitive domains, such as attention, perception, memory, and language. Lookalikes (also referred to as zoomorphic objects), inanimate objects that visually resemble animals, tend to be interpreted as animate regardless of their inanimate identity. We examined whether this animal bias can be modified through learning to understand how experience and plasticity shape visual object representations. We tested whether feedback-based categorisation training in which lookalikes had to be categorised as inanimate could reduce the animal bias. Thirty healthy participants completed three weekly sessions of animacy categorisation training, followed by an EEG recording session during which they performed an animacy task. Repeated-measures ANOVA on behavioural data revealed that categorisation efficiency, measured as the inverse efficiency score, improved both within and across sessions, but there was no evidence that this improvement was specific to lookalikes. Time-resolved multivariate pattern analysis and representational similarity analysis on EEG data obtained after this training showed a descriptively smaller animal bias relative to the no-training dataset from \citet{Chen2023}, but this reduction was not statistically significant in any analysis. Moreover, a significant animal bias was still present in participants who underwent training. Thus, neural reorganisation related to the animal bias is limited even after several training sessions to overcome this bias.

papers.title: Single-Session HRV Biofeedback Alters Neural Activity but Not Subjective Anxiety
papers.abstract: Anxiety and stress are among the most prevalent mental health concerns worldwide, yet barriers to effective treatment remain high. Biofeedback-based approaches offer a promising, low-cost complement to traditional interventions. The present study examined whether real-time heart rate variability (HRV) biofeedback enhances the efficacy of paced breathing for reducing state anxiety, and whether self-reported and neural measures of anxiety relief converge. Healthy adults completed a speeded Stroop task for stress induction, followed by a ten-minute paced breathing exercise. Participants were randomly assigned to an HRV biofeedback condition, in which real-time cardiac variability was displayed, or a control condition with the same breathing cue and no physiological feedback. State anxiety was assessed using the Spielberger State-Trait Anxiety Inventory (STAI-S), and neural activity was measured via EEG spectral power across delta, theta, alpha, and beta frequency bands. The Stroop task reliably elevated state anxiety, and paced breathing reduced STAI-S scores equivalently in both groups; HRV biofeedback did not confer additional subjective benefit. In contrast, EEG analyses revealed that the biofeedback group showed increases in delta and bilateral theta power relative to controls, and spatially widespread increases in alpha and beta power. Time-frequency analyses further showed more extensive and sustained spectral modulation in the biofeedback condition. These findings reveal a dissociation between self-reported and neural responses to a brief HRV biofeedback intervention: paced breathing alone was sufficient to reduce acute state anxiety, while HRV biofeedback produced distinct changes in neural oscillatory activity without enhancing self-reported anxiety relief. These results show that subjective anxiety recovery and neural recovery can diverge during acute HRV biofeedback, suggesting that physiological engagement with biofeedback emerges before conscious benefits.

papers.title: Light-induced melatonin suppression in school-aged children before and during camping: associations with circadian phase and daytime light exposure
papers.abstract: Prior light exposure can influence the magnitude of melatonin suppression in response to evening light, even within the same individual. We examined whether light-induced melatonin suppression in school-aged children differed before and during a camp with approximately two weeks of exposure to a natural light-dark cycle. We also explored interindividual variation in melatonin suppression and its associations with circadian phase, habitual sleep timing, and daytime light exposure. Twenty-one healthy children aged 9--14 years underwent evening light experiments at the start of camp (Pre-camp session) and approximately two weeks later (Camp session). Melatonin suppression was calculated by comparing the area under the melatonin concentration curve between the evening light condition (200 {+/-} 30 lx, 5000 K) and the dim light condition (< 30 lx, incandescent lamps), with integration starting at dim light melatonin onset (DLMO). We assessed sleep habits from 14-day sleep diaries before camping and measured wrist-level illuminance during camping. We examined associations using Spearman correlations and compared Pre-camp and Camp melatonin suppression using a paired t-test. Melatonin suppression did not differ significantly between Pre-camp and Camp sessions (p = 0.21). Greater suppression in the Pre-camp session was associated with later DLMO (rho = 0.49, p = 0.028), but not with habitual sleep variables. In the Camp session, higher same-day geometric mean illuminance was associated with lower suppression (n = 15; rho = -0.58, p = 0.024), whereas 7-day light-exposure metrics were not. Mean melatonin suppression did not significantly change across the camping period. Meanwhile, children showed large interindividual variation in melatonin suppression, and circadian phase and recent daytime light exposure are candidate correlates of this variation in the responsiveness to the evening light.

papers.title: Neural and Experiential Dynamics of High-Ventilation Breathwork Mirror Psychedelic States
papers.abstract: High-ventilation breathwork (HVB) is a simple breathing technique that nevertheless frequently triggers experiences resembling psychedelic states. While recent studies have begun to pinpoint physiological and neural changes involved in altered states of consciousness (ASCs) evoked by HVB, the interplay between neural and experiential dynamics throughout an HVB session remains unclear. Here we tracked neural activity (via 64-channel EEG recordings) as well as subjective experience depth and content in 25 experienced HVB practitioners across resting-state recordings interleaved throughout a naturalistic HVB session. We find that neural dynamics evoked by HVB emulate the most robust neural signatures of classical psychedelic states, specifically (1) loosening of temporal structure, including broadband cortical desynchronization, increased signal complexity, and decreased oscillatory power in the Alpha (8 - 13 Hz) range, and (2) reorganization of spatial structure, including a flattening of cortical processing hierarchy. These neural effects directly correlated with participants subjective depth with minute resolution, but were not explained by isolated features of HVB such as music listening or active interoception. Together, these results identify unifying neural features of psychedelic-like ASCs regardless of induction method, demonstrating that cortical states triggered by psychedelics can also be accessed by non-pharmacological routes, and breathwork is a powerful way to do so.

papers.title: Daily light exposure differences between extreme chronotypes persist after alignment to habitual sleep timing
papers.abstract: Purpose: Morning and evening chronotypes may receive light at different clock times, thereby providing differently timed signals to the circadian pacemaker. Prior studies have suggested phase-specific exposure patterns that could counter further advances in early types and delays in late types. We examined whether photoperiod modifies these exposure patterns in a way that could reasonably counteract timing extremes. Methods: We analysed near-eye melanopic equivalent daylight illuminance (EDI) in 140 participants from an international cohort across seven countries (778 participant-days; 35,949 half-hour observations). We compared four quartiles of midsleep on free days corrected for sleep debt (MSFsc) in clock time and relative to MSFsc using cyclic generalized additive mixed models, accounting for day type, site, photoperiod and individual patterns. In exploratory analyses, we tested moderation of these differences by daylength and used phase-response-curve (PRC) weighting as a conceptual comparison of exposure timing. Results: The modelled extreme evening-type/morning-type exposure ratios averaged 0.16 (95% CI 0.06-0.40) 9.6-11.3 hours before MSFsc (pre-MSFsc) and 14.0 (5.6-34.8) 0.9-4.4 hours after MSFsc (post-MSFsc). The models performed similarly well by ordinary in-sample R2 (0.795 for clock time; 0.794 for MSFsc-relative time). Pattern differences were broadly similar on work and free days, with the pre-MSFsc contrast descriptively attenuated on free days. The post-MSFsc ratio increased by a factor of 2.59 (95% CI 1.06-6.34) between civil photoperiods one hour below and above each site's average photoperiod, with no significant moderation of the pre-MSFsc contrast. Exploratory weighting by the published PRC gave higher advance-weighted point estimates in extreme evening than extreme morning types; the group difference was not statistically significant. Conclusions: Extreme chronotypes differ in daily exposure both in clock time and relative to MSFsc. The established questionnaire-based MSFsc measure showed significant post-MSFsc daylength moderation. The exposure patterns and conceptual PRC comparison suggest a possible pathway linking daylight availability to entrainment in extreme chronotypes.

papers.title: Direction of oscillatory networks in the human medial temporal lobe reverses across verbal working memory phases
papers.abstract: Working memory (WM) requires neural circuits to change how they interact as information is encoded, maintained and used. Directional oscillatory interactions in the medial temporal lobe (MTL) contribute to memory processing, but how these interactions are spatially organized during verbal WM remains unclear. Here, we analyzed intracranial electroencephalogram and neuronal spiking recorded from the human MTL during a verbal Sternberg task. Theta- and gamma-band activities in MTL showed predominant directionality in the posterior-to-anterior axis during WM encoding, but this direction was reversed to anterior-to-posterior during retrieval. Theta activities reflecting the WM load were more prevalent in left than right MTL, and theta in left MTL coordinated spike timings more strongly. Moreover, interhemispheric interactions showed a predominant left-to-right influence, with posterior-to-anterior interactions enhanced during encoding and anterior-to-posterior interactions enhanced during retrieval. Together, these findings suggest that verbal WM engages a spatially organized MTL network in which the predominant direction of oscillatory interactions changes across task phases.

papers.title: Neural dynamics track the approach to physical exhaustion
papers.abstract: Physical exhaustion has long been described through its cardiorespiratory and metabolic cost, while the neural dynamics of its approach remain largely unexplored. Here we recorded high-density electroencephalography in 28 trained cyclists during a maximal incremental test to characterise how neural dynamics change towards exhaustion. As physiological strain rose, oscillatory power shifted to lower frequencies, neural activity became more regular and predictable, and functional coupling extended to longer timescales. Participant-specific models built on neural dynamics tracked proximity to exhaustion with accuracy comparable to cardiorespiratory measures. Over the final minutes, neural features remained informative while cardiorespiratory measures lost accuracy. Models trained across participants still tracked proximity to exhaustion, but less precisely. The approach to exhaustion thus follows a common neural path, tuned to each individual.

papers.title: Electrophysiology of multisite direct electrical stimulation in the human brain
papers.abstract: Human cognition and neurological disorders reflect properties of distributed networks, yet how best to engage these networks therapeutically remains unknown. Multisite stimulation is a principled strategy for engaging brain networks, but a key translational barrier is understanding how a network combines concurrent inputs from multiple nodes. Here, we investigated the electrophysiology of simultaneous multisite direct electrical stimulation in 20 participants implanted with stereo-EEG electrodes. Synchronized dual-site stimulation engaged a larger effective network than single-site stimulation. Linear superposition explained most responses, but distinct nonlinear responses were also observed. Sublinear responses, consistent with saturation, occurred proximal to stimulation sites, while supralinear responses arose in network-connected sites during the response's late component. Moreover, low-intensity dual-site stimulation matched or exceeded single-site stimulation at higher intensities. These principles extended to three-site stimulation. These findings systematically characterize how responses to simultaneous multisite stimulation interact in the human brain, a foundational step towards principled, network-guided neurostimulation therapies.

papers.title: Repeated self-administered EEG recordings enable longitudinal measurement of brain activity at home
papers.abstract: Mobile electroencephalography (EEG) offers new opportunities to investigate brain activity outside the laboratory, but the quality and reliability of self-administered recordings remain important concerns. Here, we evaluated whether repeated at-home recordings using a four-channel consumer EEG device could provide meaningful electrophysiological measurements and characterized the stability of these measures across sessions. Five participants completed repeated recordings across multiple days, including resting-state measurements and an auditory oddball task performed with and without concurrent cognitive load. The recordings captured established spectral signatures of physiological state and task demands, including increased alpha activity during eye closure and changes in theta activity associated with cognitive load. Auditory stimulation elicited clear event-related responses, while exploratory multivariate decoding distinguished standard from target tones across recording sessions. Measurement stability varied across electrophysiological features, and aggregating repeated sessions improved the consistency of individual-level estimates. For example, split-half reliability of the auditory N1-like response increased from r = .22 with one session to r = .76 with seven sessions per half. By demonstrating the feasibility of repeated self-administered EEG measurements, this study provides a step toward investigating how brain activity varies both between individuals and within individuals over time in everyday environments.

papers.title: Nucleus reuniens gates selective hippocampal-prefrontal interactions during NREM sleep
papers.abstract: Memory consolidation requires functional synchrony between the hippocampus (HC) and the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC). The nucleus reuniens (RE) is a structural and functional hub between HC and mPFC. Here, we used in vivo electrophysiology to monitor the hippocampal-thalamic-prefrontal network in rats during non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep. We identified ripple-like activity in the RE (120 Hz peak frequency, 45 ms oscillatory duration) that occurred most frequently during NREM sleep and was associated with robust recruitment of thalamic neural spiking. RE ripple activity was phase-locked to both hippocampal sharp wave-ripples (SWR) and mPFC ripples. Although ripples were independently detected in all three structures, we found that coupling between HC and mPFC ripples mainly involved co-occurring RE ripples. These results suggest RE ripples help organize when hippocampal activity engages prefrontal circuits during sleep, with potential implications for network mechanisms of memory consolidation.
